scenes.title: Matrix quantities and dimensions
scenes.objective: Recall trace, determinant and inverse conditions.

ask.q: What condition makes a square matrix invertible?

body: For a square matrix A, the trace is the sum of diagonal entries. The determinant measures signed volume scaling and detects singularity.
A is invertible exactly when det(A) is non-zero. The inverse satisfies AA⁻¹=A⁻¹A=I. Trace is defined for every square matrix; determinant and inverse are also square-matrix concepts.
This lesson connects the computational rules with the structural identities that commonly appear in NET-JRF questions.

items.ask: What is the trace of a square matrix?
items.recall: The sum of its diagonal entries.
refresh: Trace is defined only for square matrices because it adds the diagonal entries from a single square array. For example, if A=[[1,2],[3,4]], then tr(A)=1+4=5; off-diagonal entries do not contribute.
Trace is linear: tr(A+B)=tr(A)+tr(B), and tr(cA)=c tr(A). These rules allow sums and scalar multiples to be simplified before calculating the diagonal.
Trace is also invariant under similarity. If B=P⁻¹AP, then tr(B)=tr(A); this is why diagonalisation preserves the trace and why trace equals the sum of eigenvalues with algebraic multiplicity.

items.ask: When does a square matrix have an inverse?
items.recall: Exactly when its determinant is non-zero.
refresh: A square matrix is nonsingular exactly when its determinant is non-zero. This is equivalent to full rank and to having linearly independent columns.
If det(A)=0, the homogeneous system Ax=0 has a non-zero solution, so A cannot have a two-sided inverse. Never apply an inverse formula when the determinant vanishes.
For a 2×2 matrix [[a,b],[c,d]], the determinant is ad−bc. A non-zero value guarantees the inverse exists; a zero value means the rows or columns are dependent.

items.ask: What is the determinant of a product?
refresh: The determinant is multiplicative: det(AB)=det(A)det(B). This makes a product determinant easy even when multiplying the matrices first would be tedious.
Setting B=A gives det(A²)=det(A)². If A is invertible, det(A)det(A⁻¹)=det(I)=1, so det(A⁻¹)=1/det(A).
Do not confuse multiplicativity with additivity: det(A+B) is not generally det(A)+det(B). A quick numerical counterexample is enough to rule out that false rule.

scenes.title: Trace: definition and identities
scenes.objective: Use linearity and cyclic trace identities.

blocks.body: tr(A)=Σᵢ aᵢᵢ. For compatible square products, tr(A+B)=tr(A)+tr(B), tr(cA)=c tr(A), and tr(AB)=tr(BA).
For compatible rectangular A and B, tr(AB)=tr(BA) whenever both products are square. For three factors, tr(ABC)=tr(BCA)=tr(CAB), but arbitrary reordering is not permitted.
In general AB≠BA. Trace equality does not mean the matrices themselves are equal. Trace is also similarity-invariant: tr(P⁻¹AP)=tr(A).

ask.nudge: A scalar equality is much weaker than equality of matrices.

scenario.teaser: A trace identity shortens a matrix calculation.
scenario.title: Trace shortcuts in statistical derivations
body: Statistical expressions often contain traces of matrix products such as tr(XᵀX) or tr(AB). Direct multiplication can be lengthy and hide the structure.
The cyclic property allows factors to rotate inside a trace, such as tr(ABC)=tr(BCA). It does not permit arbitrary swapping of factors.
This is useful in simplifying quadratic forms, projection matrices and covariance expressions. Keep dimensions compatible and preserve cyclic order.

scenes.title: Determinant: core properties
scenes.objective: Use determinant rules to simplify products and transformations.

blocks.body: For n×n A, det(cA)=cⁿdet(A). Swapping two rows changes sign; multiplying one row by c multiplies the determinant by c; adding a multiple of one row to another leaves it unchanged.
det(A)=0 iff rows or columns are linearly dependent iff A is singular iff A⁻¹ does not exist.

scenes.title: Guided: determinant scaling and powers
scenes.objective: Apply determinant identities to a 3×3 matrix.
scenes.problem: A is 3×3 and det(A)=2. Find det(3A), det(A²) and det(A inverse).
hints: For an invertible matrix, det(A inverse)=1/det(A).

solution.say: Since A is 3×3, det(3A)=3³×2=54. Multiplicativity gives det(A²)=2²=4. Since det(A)≠0, det(A inverse)=1/2.

ask.q: Why is the exponent 3 used in det(3A)?
ask.nudge: A has three rows, each scaled by 3.

scenario.teaser: A determinant decides whether a model matrix can be inverted.
scenario.title: Invertibility in a small linear model
body: A square model matrix is invertible exactly when its determinant is non-zero. A zero determinant means the columns are dependent and the inverse does not exist.
The determinant product rule and row-operation rules can simplify this check without a full cofactor expansion. For larger matrices, row reduction or triangular structure is often more efficient.
In statistical models, singularity signals exact linear dependence or a non-identifiable parameterisation. Check rank and determinant before writing an inverse formula.

scenes.title: Adjugate and general inverse
scenes.objective: State and apply the adjugate formula.

blocks.body: For nonsingular square A, A⁻¹=adj(A)/det(A), where adj(A) is the transpose of the cofactor matrix.
The cofactor Cᵢⱼ=(−1)ⁱ⁺ʲMᵢⱼ, where Mᵢⱼ is the minor after deleting row i and column j. The adjugate is Cᵀ.
Multiply A by the proposed inverse. The product must be I. For numerical questions, also check det(A)≠0 before applying the formula.

ask.q: For a nonsingular matrix, what is A adj(A)?
ask.nudge: It is a scalar multiple of the identity.

blocks.body: The trace equals the sum of eigenvalues and determinant equals their product, both counted with algebraic multiplicity.
Similar matrices have the same characteristic polynomial, trace, determinant and eigenvalues. If B=P⁻¹AP, then det(B)=det(A) and tr(B)=tr(A).

scenes.title: Trace is cyclic, not commutative
scenes.objective: Distinguish cyclic invariance from arbitrary factor reordering.

ask.q: Does tr(ABC)=tr(ACB) hold for all matrices?

body: Trace has a special cyclic property: tr(ABC)=tr(BCA)=tr(CAB), provided the products are defined. This is not the same as saying matrix multiplication is commutative.
The matrices AB and BA can be different even though their traces agree. When simplifying longer products, rotate the entire product without changing the order of the factors.
